claims.claim: In the academic study of religion, myth is an analytical term: a sacred or foundational narrative that a community regards as true and meaningful, not a synonym for a false story.

The Greek mythos meant word, saying, or story; for archaic Greeks a muthos was a true story that unveils the true origin of the world and human beings, whereas in modern everyday speech myth usually means a belief that is in fact false — a pejorative shift scholars trace.

Folkloristics classifies prose narratives into myth (a sacred narrative of the remote past, regarded as true), legend (a narrative about human beings in historical time, which may also be regarded as true), and folktale (fiction told for entertainment, not regarded as true); a classic formulation is folklorist William Bascom's 1965 study of prose narrative forms.

Cosmogonic (creation) myths narrate the beginning of the world as a particular community understands it, orient the community within reality, and are treated in creation-myth scholarship as foundational: other cultural myths and forms take their model from the cosmogonic myth.
Etiological myths explain how a particular custom, technique, or feature of the world came to be, and are distinct from cosmogonic myths, which deal with the ultimate origin of all things.

Charter myths authorize practices, institutions, and moral order: Bronislaw Malinowski argued that myth, studied in living communities, is not an idle tale or an intellectual explanation but 'a pragmatic charter of primitive faith and moral wisdom' — it expresses, enhances, and codifies belief, safeguards and enforces morality, vouches for the efficiency of ritual, and contains practical rules for the guidance of man.

Mircea Eliade argued that myth represents the absolute truth about primordial time, that 'myth, then, is always an account of a creation,' and that recounting or re-enacting a myth re-actualizes the primordial events (sacred time, illud tempus); later scholars noted the idea became a truism in the study of religions.

Eliade's sacred-time theory drew scholarly critique: classicist G. S. Kirk judged it a valuable insight into certain myths rather than a universal key to all mythology, and other scholars criticized overgeneralization, limited empirical support, and insufficient attention to historical and cultural context.

Myth and ritual are related but distinct: ritual is often the dramatic presentation of a myth, and myth can vouch for a ritual's efficacy; the precise relationship is a debated scholarly question, and ritual is treated as its own topic in this curriculum.

Religious narratives, symbols, and traditions commonly function to give life meaning and to help people understand the universe; religion is studied sociologically as beliefs, practices, norms, and group life.

Descriptive academic study distinguishes reporting what participants say, do, and regard as true from confessional or prescriptive claims, which supports reading myths with insider and outsider perspectives held apart and without adjudicating truth.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does 'myth' necessarily mean a religious narrative?
positions: Everyday speech uses myth for any false or unverifiable belief, religious or not (a pejorative sense).
In folkloristics and religious studies, myth denotes a sacred narrative of the remote past, with no implication about its truth.
Some scholars extend 'myth' to secular ideologies and modern narratives.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the religious-studies sense as its working definition, notes the everyday pejorative sense and its history, and names the term's wider uses only to set them aside.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What is the relationship between myth and ritual?
positions: Myth-ritual theories (e.g., early comparative religion) hold that myths explain or script rituals.
Malinowski treats myth as vouching for ritual's efficacy and grounding practice.
Eliade treats recounting and re-enacting myth as re-actualizing sacred time.
Other scholars caution that many myths have no ritual counterpart and many rituals no myth.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states that myth and ritual are related but distinct, gives the dramatization and re-actualization framings briefly, and refers to the ritual sibling topic for depth.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is Eliade's sacred-time theory valid for all myths?
positions: Eliade proposed it as a general account of traditional religious myth (myth as account of a creation; re-actualization of sacred time).
G. S. Kirk and others argued it overgeneralizes and lacks empirical and contextual grounding; some specialists dismissed Eliade's works.
Defenders (e.g., Wendy Doniger) call the theory a useful starting point for comparative study even where not universally applicable.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents Eliade's framing with attribution, names the scholarly critique, and does not present either side as settled.

sourceRecords.title: Myth | Definition, History, Examples, & Facts
sourceRecords.notes: Britannica blocks automated fetch; read via Internet Archive captures of 2025-06-01 and 2023-01-04 (canonical URL registered). The captures contain the article lead, which defines myth as a symbolic narrative, usually of unknown origin and at least partly traditional, that ostensibly relates actual events and is especially associated with religious belief; states that every myth presents itself as an authoritative, factual account; traces mythos from 'word' and 'saying' through 'story' to 'fiction' in contrast with logos; and says the study of religion must distinguish myths from stories that are merely untrue. The article's structure (Relation of myths to other narrative forms: fables, fairy tales, folktales, sagas and epics, legends, parables, etiologic tales; Approaches including folkloric and functionalist) corroborates the folkloristics taxonomy. Reference only; original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Creation Myth | Definition, Types, Examples, & Facts
sourceRecords.notes: Britannica blocks automated fetch; read the full article text via Internet Archive capture of 2023-10-30 (canonical URL registered). Supports: creation myth (cosmogonic myth) as the symbolic narrative of the beginning of the world as understood by a particular community; myth as imaginative expression in narrative form of what is experienced or apprehended as basic reality; the cosmogonic myth as the foundational myth that models other cultural myths and orients a community within reality; the distinction between cosmogonic and etiological myths; ritual as often the dramatic presentation of myth; and the notion of a sacred or real time established by the cosmogonic myth. Reference only; original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Myth in Primitive Psychology (1926), by Bronislaw Malinowski
sourceRecords.provider: Internet Archive (scan of the W. W. Norton edition)
sourceRecords.notes: Read the full-text OCR (djvu.txt) of the Internet Archive scan on 2026-08-21; the work was published in 1926 and is in the public domain. Primary scholarly source. Supports Malinowski's charter-function argument: myth studied in living communities is not an idle tale but a hard-worked active force; it is 'not an intellectual explanation or an artistic imagery, but a pragmatic charter of primitive faith and moral wisdom'; myth expresses, enhances, and codifies belief, safeguards and enforces morality, vouches for the efficiency of ritual, and contains practical rules for the guidance of man; Malinowski also distinguishes myth from fairy tale, legend, and historical record. One short attributed quotation used; otherwise original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Myth — Wikipedia
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21 as a Tier D reputable secondary source. Supports: the folkloristics classification of myth (sacred narrative of the remote past), legend (human protagonists, historical time), and folktale (not regarded as true, told for entertainment); the widely cited definition by folklorist Lauri Honko (myth as a story of the gods, a religious account of the beginning of the world, expressing and confirming society's religious values and providing patterns of behavior); folklorists' use of 'myth' without implication about truth; the pejorative colloquial sense that arose from labeling other cultures' beliefs incorrect; origin/charter myths as accounts of how customs, institutions, and taboos were established; and the myth-ritual relationship as a scholarly question. The article's references cite Bascom 1965 for the prose-narrative classification. Facts cross-checked against the Tier A/B sources; original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Mircea Eliade — Wikipedia
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21 as a Tier D reputable secondary source for attributed scholarly framings. Supports: Eliade's account that in traditional societies myth represents the absolute truth about primordial time, that myth is always an account of a creation, that the mythical age is sacred time, and that recounting or re-enacting myth re-actualizes the primordial events (the 'eternal return'); Wendy Doniger's observation that the idea became a truism in the study of religions; and the scholarly critique of Eliade, including G. S. Kirk's judgment that the sacred-time idea is a valuable perception about certain myths rather than a guide to the proper understanding of all of them, plus criticisms of overgeneralization, limited empirical support, and insufficient attention to historical and cultural context. Facts synthesized in original prose; Eliade's biography and politics are out of scope for the lesson.
